question: Did halving the size of each BVH node, by storing its box coordinates as small integers, make the walk faster?
answer:
No — halving the BVH node made the walk measurably slower, so I rejected it.

What I tried: each node's six box coordinates were stored as 16-bit integers (float(u16) is exact for our quantization grid, so the arithmetic is unchanged) plus the 4-byte payload, giving one 16-byte node fetched with a single uint4 load instead of two float4 loads of a 32-byte node.

Why it is a fair comparison: the variant produced a byte-identical PFM to the round-7 baseline on all three scenes (scene-default, scene-alt-view, scene-caustic-closeup) at 64 spp, seed 1, and printed samples = 512*512*64.

Measured result (interleaved paired A/B, 16 pairs, 64 spp, default scene): 0/16 wins, mean delta +0.2796 ms, geometric-mean ratio 1.00900 (+0.90%), sd_log 0.00221, t = +16.25 — i.e. a consistent ~0.9% regression, not noise.

Interpretation: the traversal is ALU/latency-bound, not node-bandwidth-bound. Unpacking costs about six mask/shift/convert ops per node visited, and that overhead exceeds the bandwidth saved by moving half the bytes. This is consistent with round 7, where simply deleting a float->int conversion (no layout change) was worth -0.44%, and with my round-8 cost profile showing the trace kernel is 98.6% of GPU time while the memory traffic is small. The candidate is preserved in _r8_node16/ for reference; the shipped tree was reverted to round-7 code and re-verified byte-identical.

question: Did halving the size of each BVH node, by storing its box coordinates as small integers, make the walk faster?
answer:
No — halving the BVH node made it measurably slower.

What I tried (round 8, experiment E5): the round-7 node is 32 bytes (two float4 halves: lo[4] + hi[4]) and is read as two dependent 16-byte loads. I replaced it with a 16-byte node holding the six box coordinates as 16-bit integers plus a 4-byte payload, so a node costs one uint4 load. Because the host quantizes with a power-of-two scale and clamps coordinates to <= 65535, float(u16) reconstructs the exact same float32 bounds, so the traversal decisions are provably unchanged — I confirmed the PFM is byte-identical to round 7 on all three scenes (scene-default, scene-alt-view, scene-caustic-closeup) at 512x512, 64 spp, seed 1.

Measured result: interleaved paired A/B, 16 pairs, --benchmark 5 per pass, 64 spp, default scene, candidate vs the frozen round-7 binary — candidate won 0/16 pairs, mean_delta = +0.2796 ms, geo_mean_ratio = 1.00900 (+0.90% slower), sd_log = 0.00221, t = +16.25. That is a very confident regression, not noise.

Why it loses: the saved memory traffic is smaller than the ALU it costs. Each node test now needs six unpack steps (mask, shift, integer-to-float convert) before the slab test can start, and the walk is latency/ALU-bound on the critical path, not bandwidth-bound. Two independent results support that diagnosis: round 7 gained -0.44% just by deleting the uint-to-float conversion (going the other direction, u16 -> f32 in the same 32-byte node), and my cost profile shows the trace dispatch is 98.6% of GPU time with only ~1% of peak FLOPs used, i.e. stalls and dependent-op latency dominate.

Status: the 16-byte node is rejected and preserved in _r8_node16/; pathtracer/ was reverted from the frozen _r8b copy and re-verified byte-identical. Evidence is in the writer log's round-8 section and my working-memory entry 'r8-rejected-e5-e3-e4'.
